What is the equivalent provision for Murder (Section 302 IPC) under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS)?
response: Under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS), the offence of murder is defined under Section 101 BNS (corresponding to Section 300 IPC) and the punishment for murder is prescribed under Section 103 BNS (corresponding to Section 302 IPC). Section 103(1) BNS prescribes the sentence of death or imprisonment for life, and liability to fine. Furthermore, Section 103(2) BNS specifically penalizes mob lynching or murder committed by five or more persons on grounds of race, caste, sex, place of birth, or religion with death or life imprisonment.

instruction: Which section of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) corresponds to Cheating under Section 420 IPC?
response: Section 420 of the Indian Penal Code (Cheating and dishonestly inducing delivery of property) corresponds to Section 318(4) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS). Under Section 318(4) BNS, whoever cheats and thereby dishonestly induces the person deceived to deliver any property is punishable with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.

instruction: Identify the corresponding provision for Anticipatory Bail in the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS).
response: Section 438 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (CrPC) regarding Anticipatory Bail corresponds to Section 482 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS). Section 482 BNSS retains the power of the High Court and Sessions Court to grant pre-arrest direction for bail where a person apprehends arrest in a non-bailable offence, incorporating statutory factors and conditions to prevent misuse.

instruction: Which section of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) corresponds to Inherent Powers under Section 482 CrPC?
response: The inherent powers of the High Court previously enshrined under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (CrPC) are now preserved under Section 528 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS). Section 528 BNSS states that nothing in the Sanhita shall be deemed to limit or affect the inherent powers of the High Court to make such orders as may be necessary to give effect to any order, or to prevent abuse of the process of any court, or otherwise to secure the ends of justice.

instruction: How are electronic records treated under Section 61 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) compared to Section 65B of the Indian Evidence Act?
response: Section 61 and Section 63 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) replace the provisions of Section 65A and Section 65B of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872. Under BSA, electronic records are given primary status equivalent to physical documents. Section 63 BSA prescribes the conditions for admissibility of electronic records, recognizing digital signatures, hash algorithms, cloud records, and metadata, providing a modernized certificate framework akin to Section 65B(4) IEA.

instruction: Explain the zero FIR concept and preliminary enquiry under Section 173 BNSS.
response: Section 173 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) statutorily codifies 'Zero FIR', mandating that information regarding a cognizable offence can be provided to any police station irrespective of territorial jurisdiction. If recorded elsewhere, it must be transferred to the jurisdictional police station within 15 days. Additionally, Section 173(3) BNSS statutorily authorizes a preliminary enquiry for offences punishable with 3 to 7 years imprisonment within 14 days with prior permission of a DSP to ascertain whether a prima facie case exists.

instruction: Summarize the landmark principles laid down in Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar (2014) regarding arrest.
response: In Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar (2014) 8 SCC 273, the Supreme Court issued mandatory directions to police and magistrates to prevent unnecessary arrests in offences punishable with imprisonment of seven years or less (including Section 498A IPC). The Court mandated: (1) Police officers must not automatically arrest without satisfying Section 41 CrPC requirements; (2) A notice of appearance under Section 41A CrPC must be served within 14 days of filing the case; (3) Magistrates must record reasons before authorising detention; (4) Failure to comply renders the police officer liable for contempt of court and departmental action.

instruction: What are the eleven mandatory custody guidelines established in D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal (1997)?
response: In D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal (1997) 1 SCC 416, the Supreme Court formulated mandatory safeguards against custodial violence and torture: (1) Arresting officers must display clear identification tags; (2) Preparation of an Arrest Memo witnessed by at least one family member or respectable local citizen; (3) Right of the arrestee to have a friend or relative informed within 8 to 12 hours; (4) Recording entries in the general diary; (5) Right to medical examination upon arrest and every 48 hours during custody; (6) Right to consult a lawyer during interrogation; (7) Forwarding copies of arrest documents to the Magistrate.

instruction: Summarize the legal ratio in Lalita Kumari v. Government of U.P. (2014) regarding FIR registration.
response: In Lalita Kumari v. Govt. of U.P. (2014) 2 SCC 1, a 5-judge Constitution Bench held that registration of an FIR is mandatory under Section 154 CrPC if the information discloses the commission of a cognizable offence, and no preliminary enquiry is permissible in such cases. If the information does not disclose a cognizable offence but indicates the necessity of an enquiry, a preliminary enquiry may be conducted only to ascertain whether a cognizable offence is disclosed. Such enquiry must be time-bound and concluded within 7 days in areas such as matrimonial disputes, commercial offences, medical negligence, corruption, or abnormal delay cases.

instruction: Explain the five golden principles (Panchsheel) of circumstantial evidence in Sharad Birdhichand Sarda v. State of Maharashtra (1984).
response: In Sharad Birdhichand Sarda v. State of Maharashtra (1984) 4 SCC 116, the Supreme Court laid down five golden principles (Panchsheel) for convicting on circumstantial evidence: (1) The circumstances from which the conclusion of guilt is drawn must be fully established; (2) The facts established must be consistent only with the hypothesis of the guilt of the accused; (3) The circumstances must be of a conclusive nature and tendency; (4) They must exclude every possible hypothesis except the one to be proved; (5) There must be a chain of evidence so complete as not to leave any reasonable ground for innocence, showing that the act must have been done by the accused.

instruction: What are the governing guidelines for quashing an FIR laid down in State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal (1992)?
response: In State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal 1992 Supp (1) SCC 335, the Supreme Court identified seven illustrative categories for exercising inherent powers under Section 482 CrPC to quash an FIR: (1) Where the allegations in the FIR, taken at face value, do not prima facie constitute any offence; (2) Where the uncontroverted allegations do not disclose a cognizable offence; (3) Where uncontroverted evidence does not disclose the commission of any offence; (4) Where the offence is non-cognizable without Magistrate order under Section 155(2); (5) Where allegations are absurd and inherently improbable; (6) Where there is an express legal bar under CrPC or special law; (7) Where the criminal proceeding is manifestly attended with mala fides.

instruction: Summarize the holding in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) regarding Section 66A of the IT Act.
response: In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, the Supreme Court struck down Section 66A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 in its entirety as unconstitutional. The Court held that Section 66A violated freedom of speech and expression guaranteed under Article 19(1)(a) and was not saved by reasonable restrictions under Article 19(2). The provisions suffered from fatal vagueness, overbreadth, and created a chilling effect on legitimate online speech, failing to distinguish between mere advocacy, discussion, and actual incitement to violence.

instruction: Explain the ratio in Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India (2018) regarding Section 377 IPC.
response: In Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India (2018) 1 SCC 1, a 5-judge Constitution Bench read down Section 377 of the Indian Penal Code to decriminalize consensual sexual acts between adults of the same sex in private. The Court held that criminalizing consensual sexual conduct violated Articles 14 (equality), 15 (non-discrimination on grounds of sex), 19(1)(a) (expression), and 21 (right to dignity, privacy, and personal autonomy). Section 377 remains valid only for non-consensual sexual acts, sex with minors, and bestiality.

instruction: Explain the Doctrine of Res Judicata under Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.
response: Section 11 CPC codifies the Doctrine of Res Judicata ('a matter judged'). It provides that no Court shall try any suit or issue in which the matter directly and substantially in issue has been directly and substantially in issue in a former suit between the same parties, or between parties under whom they or any of them claim, litigating under the same title, in a Court competent to try such subsequent suit, and has been heard and finally decided by such Court. It is founded on public policy: nemo debet bis vexari pro una et eadem causa (no person should be vexed twice for the same cause) and interest reipublicae ut sit finis litium (it is in the state's interest that there be an end to litigation).

instruction: What is Constructive Res Judicata under Explanation IV to Section 11 CPC?
response: Explanation IV to Section 11 CPC embodies the rule of Constructive Res Judicata. It provides that any matter which might and ought to have been made a ground of defence or attack in a former suit shall be deemed to have been a matter directly and substantially in issue in such suit. Consequently, if a party failed to raise a plea which was available to them and ought to have been raised, they are precluded from agitating that plea in a subsequent suit, even if it was not expressly adjudicated previously.

instruction: What is the difference between Res Judicata (Section 11 CPC) and Res Sub Judice (Section 10 CPC)?
response: Section 10 CPC (Res Sub Judice) deals with the stay of a subsequently instituted suit when a previously instituted suit between the same parties involving the same matter in issue is pending in a competent court; it prevents concurrent parallel trials. Section 11 CPC (Res Judicata) deals with barring a subsequent suit when the matter in issue has already been heard and finally decided in a former suit by a competent court; it prevents re-litigation of decided matters.

instruction: What is the scope of Section 27 of the Indian Evidence Act regarding discovery of facts?
response: Section 27 of the Indian Evidence Act (and Section 23 of BSA) is an exception to the ban on police confessions under Sections 25 and 26. It provides that when any fact is deposed to as discovered in consequence of information received from a person accused of an offence in police custody, so much of such information, whether it amounts to a confession or not, as relates distinctly to the fact thereby discovered, may be proved. In Pulukuri Kottaya (1947), the Privy Council clarified that only the information directly leading to the physical recovery of the object/fact is admissible, and narrative confessions of guilt remain excluded.

instruction: What are the statutory presumptions under Sections 118 and 139 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881?
response: Section 118(a) of the NI Act creates a statutory presumption that every negotiable instrument was made or drawn for consideration. Section 139 mandates that the court shall presume, unless the contrary is proved, that the holder of a cheque received it for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability. In Rangappa v. Sri Mohan (2010), the Supreme Court held that Section 139 includes the existence of a legally enforceable debt. The accused can rebut this presumption on a preponderance of probabilities by raising a probable defence.

instruction: What are the essential conditions for invoking Section 9 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996?
response: Section 9 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 empowers a party to apply to a Court for interim measures of protection: (1) before the commencement of arbitral proceedings; (2) during arbitral proceedings; or (3) after the making of the arbitral award but before enforcement. Under Section 9(2), if interim relief is granted prior to commencement, arbitral proceedings must be commenced within 90 days from the date of such order. The court applies the prima facie case, balance of convenience, and irreparable injury tests.

instruction: Explain the concept of an Order of Reference under Section 8 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996.
response: Section 8 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 mandates that a judicial authority before which an action is brought in a matter which is the subject of an arbitration agreement shall refer the parties to arbitration, provided a party applies not later than the date of submitting their first statement on the substance of the dispute, accompanied by the original arbitration agreement or certified copy. Following the 2015 amendment, the judicial authority's scrutiny is confined to examining whether prima facie a valid arbitration agreement exists.

instruction: What is a Summary Suit under Order XXXVII of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908?
response: Order XXXVII CPC provides a summary procedure for speedy adjudication of debt recovery and commercial claims arising out of bills of exchange, hundis, promissory notes, or written contracts with liquidated sums. The defendant is not entitled to defend the suit as of right; they must enter an appearance within 10 days of summons. The plaintiff then serves a Summons for Judgment, and the defendant must seek 'leave to defend' within 10 days by demonstrating a triable, bona fide issue. If leave is refused, plaintiff is entitled to judgment immediately.

instruction: What constitutes 'Cruelty' as a ground for divorce under Section 13(1)(ia) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955?
response: Under Section 13(1)(ia) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, cruelty may be either physical or mental. In Samar Ghosh v. Jaya Ghosh (2007) 4 SCC 511, the Supreme Court held that mental cruelty involves conduct of such grave character that the petitioner cannot reasonably be expected to live with the respondent. It must be assessed in light of the parties' background, educational status, and social norms. Persistent denial of physical relationship, false criminal complaints leading to arrest, and continuous indignities constitute mental cruelty.

instruction: What are the essential elements of Criminal Conspiracy under Section 120A of the Indian Penal Code?
response: Section 120A IPC defines Criminal Conspiracy as an agreement between two or more persons to do, or cause to be done: (1) an illegal act; or (2) an act which is not illegal by illegal means. Where the agreement is to commit an offence, the agreement itself is sufficient and no overt act is necessary. Where the agreement is to do an act which is not an offence, an overt act in pursuance of the agreement is required. Punishment is provided under Section 120B IPC.

instruction: What are the rights of an arrested person under Section 50 and 50A of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973?
response: Section 50 CrPC confers two vital statutory rights: (1) Every police officer arresting without a warrant must forthwith communicate to the arrestee full particulars of the offence or other grounds for arrest; (2) In non-bailable cases, the officer must inform the person that they are entitled to be released on bail and may arrange sureties. Section 50A mandates that the police officer must immediately inform a nominated friend, relative, or person of the arrest and the place where they are held, and make an entry thereof in the police station register.

instruction: What are the essentials of Section 65B of the Indian Evidence Act for electronic evidence admissibility?
response: In Arjun Panditrao Khotkar v. Kailash Kushanrao Gorantyal (2020) 7 SCC 1, the Supreme Court clarified that a certificate under Section 65B(4) of the Indian Evidence Act is a condition precedent to the admissibility of secondary electronic evidence (such as CDs, pen drives, printouts). The certificate must: (1) identify the electronic record; (2) describe the manner of its production; (3) give particulars of the device used; and (4) be signed by a person occupying an official responsible position in relation to the device or management of the relevant activity.

instruction: Explain the Doctrine of Promissory Estoppel in Indian Administrative Law.
response: In Motilal Padampat Sugar Mills v. State of U.P. (1979) 2 SCC 409, the Supreme Court established the Doctrine of Promissory Estoppel against the Government. When the Government makes a clear and unequivocal representation or promise intending to create legal relations, and a citizen alters their position relying on that promise, the Government cannot resile from that promise. It is an equitable doctrine enforceable even in the absence of a formal contract, subject to supervening public interest.

instruction: What is the difference between Cognizable and Non-Cognizable offences under Section 2(c) and 2(l) CrPC?
response: Under Section 2(c) CrPC, a 'cognizable offence' is one in which a police officer may, in accordance with the First Schedule or other law, arrest without a warrant and investigate without an order of a Magistrate under Section 156(1). Under Section 2(l) CrPC, a 'non-cognizable offence' is one in which a police officer has no authority to arrest without warrant and cannot investigate without the prior order of a Magistrate under Section 155(2).

instruction: Explain the concept of Default Bail (Compulsive Bail) under Section 167(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
response: Section 167(2) CrPC provides an indefeasible statutory right to default bail if the investigating agency fails to file a charge-sheet within the prescribed period: (1) 90 days for offences punishable with death, life imprisonment, or imprisonment not less than 10 years; (2) 60 days for all other offences. In Bikramjit Singh v. State of Punjab (2020), the Supreme Court held that the right to default bail is a fundamental right flowing from Article 21. Once the accused applies for default bail upon expiry of the period, the subsequent filing of a charge-sheet does not defeat this right.

instruction: What is a Dying Declaration and what are its requirements under Section 32(1) of the Indian Evidence Act?
response: A Dying Declaration under Section 32(1) of the Indian Evidence Act is a statement made by a person as to the cause of their death, or as to any of the circumstances of the transaction which resulted in their death, in cases in which the cause of that person's death comes into question. In Laxman v. State of Maharashtra (2002), the Constitution Bench held that a dying declaration can form the sole basis of conviction without corroboration if the court is satisfied that it is true, voluntary, and the declarant was in a fit mental state to make the statement.

instruction: What are the rules regarding Test Identification Parade (TIP) under Section 9 of the Indian Evidence Act and Section 54A CrPC?
response: A Test Identification Parade (TIP) is conducted during investigation to enable a witness to identify an accused not previously known to them. It is governed by Section 9 IEA and Section 54A CrPC. TIP is not substantive evidence; its purpose is to corroborate the witness's substantive dock identification in court. Failure to hold TIP without justification may weaken the prosecution case, but delay or absence is not fatal if the witness had ample opportunity to observe the accused during the crime.

instruction: What constitutes 'Cheating' under Section 415 of the Indian Penal Code?
response: Under Section 415 IPC, Cheating requires: (1) Deception of any person; (2) Fraudulently or dishonestly inducing the person deceived to deliver any property, or consent that any person shall retain property; or (3) Intentionally inducing the person deceived to do or omit to do anything which they would not do/omit if not deceived, causing harm in body, mind, reputation, or property. A mere failure to fulfill a promise does not constitute cheating unless fraudulent intent existed at the inception of the contract.

instruction: What is the distinction between Theft (Section 378 IPC) and Extortion (Section 383 IPC)?
response: The distinctions are: (1) In Theft (Section 378 IPC), property is taken dishonestly without the consent of the owner; in Extortion (Section 383 IPC), consent is obtained by intentionally putting a person in fear of injury; (2) Theft applies exclusively to movable property; Extortion applies to both movable and immovable property or anything that can be converted into a valuable security; (3) In Theft, there is no element of coercion or fear; Extortion requires delivery of property induced by fear.

instruction: Explain the concept of 'Robbery' and when Theft or Extortion becomes Robbery under Section 390 IPC.
response: Under Section 390 IPC, in all robbery there is either theft or extortion. Theft is robbery if, in order to the committing of the theft, or in committing the theft, or in carrying away property obtained by the theft, the offender causes or attempts to cause to any person death, hurt, or wrongful restraint, or fear of instant death, hurt, or wrongful restraint. Extortion is robbery if the offender, at the time of committing it, is in the presence of the person put in fear, and commits extortion by putting that person in fear of instant death, instant hurt, or instant wrongful restraint.

instruction: What is the defence of Private Defence of body under Section 96 to 100 IPC?
response: Section 96 IPC provides that nothing is an offence which is done in the exercise of the right of private defence. Section 97 extends this right to defend one's own body and the body of any other person. Section 99 limits this right: it does not extend to inflicting more harm than is necessary, nor where recourse to public authorities is available. Section 100 IPC enumerates seven situations where private defence of body extends to voluntarily causing death, including reasonable apprehension of death, grievous hurt, rape, unnatural lust, kidnapping/abduction, and acid attacks.

instruction: What is the procedure for execution of a decree under Order XXI of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908?
response: Order XXI CPC is the most comprehensive procedural order, governing execution of decrees. Modes of execution under Section 51 and Order XXI include: (1) Delivery of specific property; (2) Attachment and sale of property (Rule 54); (3) Arrest and detention in civil prison (Rule 37-40); (4) Appointment of a receiver; (5) Delivery of possession in partition or eviction suits. A judgment-debtor cannot resist execution on grounds which could have been raised in the suit.

instruction: What are the conditions for granting an Injunction under Section 38 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963?
response: Section 38 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 governs Perpetual (Permanent) Injunctions. A perpetual injunction may be granted to the plaintiff to prevent the breach of an obligation existing in their favour: (1) where the defendant is trustee of the property; (2) where there exists no standard for ascertaining actual damage; (3) where pecuniary compensation would not afford adequate relief; (4) where the injunction is necessary to prevent a multiplicity of judicial proceedings.

instruction: Explain Section 14 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 regarding contracts that cannot be specifically enforced.
response: Following the 2018 amendment, Section 14 enumerates four categories of contracts that cannot be specifically enforced: (a) where a party has obtained substituted performance under Section 20; (b) a contract the performance of which involves performance of a continuous duty which the court cannot supervise; (c) a contract so dependent on the personal qualifications of the parties that the court cannot enforce specific performance of its material terms (e.g. personal service contracts); (d) a contract which is in its nature determinable.

instruction: What is the legal effect of an unstamped or under-stamped document under Section 35 of the Indian Stamp Act, 1899?
response: Section 35 of the Indian Stamp Act, 1899 provides that no instrument chargeable with duty shall be admitted in evidence for any purpose, or acted upon, registered, or authenticated by any public officer, unless it is duly stamped. In N.N. Global Mercantile (2023 5-judge bench), overruled by the 7-judge Constitution Bench in Re: Interplay Between Arbitration Agreements and the Stamp Act (2023), the Supreme Court held that an unstamped arbitration agreement is not void ab initio; rather, non-stamping is a curable defect that does not prevent appointment of an arbitrator under Section 11 of the Arbitration Act.

instruction: What is the territorial jurisdiction of Civil Courts under Section 16 to 20 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908?
response: Under CPC: Section 16 mandates that suits relating to immovable property (recovery, partition, mortgage foreclosure, determination of rights) must be instituted in the court within whose local limits the property is situate. Section 17 governs property situate across multiple jurisdictions. Section 19 covers suits for wrongs to person or movables. Section 20 is the residuary section: suits must be instituted where the defendant resides, carries on business, or personally works for gain, or where the cause of action wholly or in part arises.

instruction: What is the difference between Section 156(3) CrPC and Section 200 CrPC?
response: Under Section 156(3) CrPC, a Magistrate empowers the police to register an FIR and investigate a cognizable case at the pre-cognizance stage; the police submit a report under Section 173. Under Section 200 CrPC, a Magistrate takes cognizance of an offence upon receiving a private complaint and proceeds to examine the complainant and witnesses upon oath. If a prima facie case is made out under Section 204, process is issued; otherwise, the complaint is dismissed under Section 203.

instruction: What is the effect of compounding an offence under Section 320 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973?
response: Section 320 CrPC governs the compounding of offences. Subsection (1) lists offences compoundable without court permission (e.g. hurt under Section 323 IPC, simple defamation); subsection (2) lists offences compoundable only with the permission of the court. Under Section 320(8) CrPC, the statutory composition of an offence has the legal effect of an acquittal of the accused with whom the offence has been compounded, extinguishing criminal liability completely.

instruction: Explain the ingredients of cruelty by husband or relatives under Section 498A IPC.
response: Section 498A IPC penalizes cruelty by a husband or relative of the husband towards a woman with imprisonment up to three years and fine. Cruelty means: (a) any wilful conduct likely to drive the woman to commit suicide or cause grave injury or danger to life, limb, or mental/physical health; or (b) harassment with a view to coercing her or her relatives to meet any unlawful demand for property or valuable security.

instruction: What is the purpose of maintenance proceedings under Section 125 CrPC?
response: Section 125 CrPC is a summary, social justice measure intended to prevent vagrancy and destitution. It empowers a Magistrate to order a person having sufficient means to pay a monthly maintenance allowance to their wife (unable to maintain herself), legitimate or illegitimate minor children, and parents unable to maintain themselves. It is preventive rather than punitive in nature.

instruction: What is the procedure for recording confessions and statements under Section 164 CrPC?
response: Under Section 164 CrPC, a Metropolitan or Judicial Magistrate may record any confession or statement made to them in the course of an investigation. For confessions: (1) The Magistrate must explain to the person that they are not bound to confess; (2) Warn them that any confession made may be used as evidence against them; (3) Satisfy themselves that it is made voluntarily; (4) Ensure the person is not kept in police custody prior to recording; (5) Record a statutory memorandum of voluntariness at the foot.

instruction: Under what grounds can a Plaint be rejected under Order VII Rule 11 CPC?
response: Order VII Rule 11 CPC mandates rejection of a plaint on six statutory grounds: (a) where it does not disclose a cause of action; (b) where relief claimed is undervalued and plaintiff fails to correct valuation; (c) where plaint is insufficiently stamped and plaintiff fails to supply requisite stamps; (d) where the suit appears from the statement in the plaint to be barred by any law; (e) where plaint is not filed in duplicate; (f) where plaintiff fails to comply with statutory provisions regarding service. Rejection is based solely on plaint averments without looking at the written statement.

instruction: What constitutes Rioting armed with deadly weapon under Section 148 IPC?
response: Section 148 IPC punishes rioting being armed with a deadly weapon or anything which, used as a weapon of offence, is likely to cause death, with imprisonment up to three years or fine or both. The essential ingredients are: (1) Formation of an unlawful assembly of five or more persons; (2) Use of force or violence by the assembly in prosecution of a common object; (3) The accused was personally armed with a deadly weapon at the time of rioting.

instruction: Distinguish between Common Intention (Section 34 IPC) and Criminal Conspiracy (Section 120B IPC).
response: Common Intention (Section 34) requires a pre-arranged plan and active physical or overt participation in the commission of the offence; it is a rule of joint liability. Criminal Conspiracy (Section 120B) is a distinct substantive offence; the mere agreement to commit an offence constitutes the offence without requiring physical participation or execution of the act.

instruction: Explain the purpose and mandatory nature of examination of accused under Section 313 CrPC.
response: Section 313 CrPC embodies the principle of natural justice (audi alteram partem). Its purpose is to enable the accused personally to explain any incriminating circumstances appearing in the prosecution evidence against them. The Court must question the accused generally on the case without administering oath. Incriminating evidence not put to the accused under Section 313 cannot be used against them in judgment.

instruction: What is the statutory obligation of the Magistrate under Section 207 CrPC regarding supply of police report copies?
response: Section 207 CrPC mandates that in any case instituted on a police report, the Magistrate shall without delay furnish to the accused, free of cost, copies of: (1) the police report (charge-sheet); (2) the FIR under Section 154; (3) statements of all witnesses recorded under Section 161(3); (4) confessions and statements recorded under Section 164; and (5) any other document forwarded to the Magistrate under Section 173(5). This ensures a fair trial.

instruction: Explain preventative detention powers under Section 107 and 151 CrPC.
response: Section 107 CrPC authorizes an Executive Magistrate to require a person to show cause why they should not execute a bond with or without sureties for keeping the peace for up to one year, if information is received that the person is likely to commit a breach of the peace. Section 151 CrPC empowers a police officer knowing of a design to commit any cognizable offence to arrest the person without warrant to prevent the commission of the offence, provided detention cannot exceed 24 hours without Magistrate authority.

instruction: What is the procedure and protection provided under Section 41A CrPC?
response: Section 41A CrPC mandates that in offences where arrest is not mandatory under Section 41(1) (offences punishable up to 7 years), the police officer shall issue a notice directing the person against whom a reasonable complaint has been made to appear before them. Where the person complies with and continues to comply with the notice, they shall not be arrested unless the police officer records reasons that arrest is necessary and obtains judicial sanction.

instruction: Explain the legal provision, essential ingredients, and court principles regarding Section 311 CrPC (Power of Court to summon material witness or examine person present).
response: Section 311 CrPC confers discretionary power on any court at any stage of inquiry or trial to summon any person as a witness, examine any person in attendance, or recall and re-examine any person already examined. The second part is mandatory: the court shall summon and examine or recall if their evidence appears essential to the just decision of the case.

instruction: Explain the legal provision, essential ingredients, and court principles regarding Section 319 CrPC (Power to proceed against other persons appearing to be guilty of offence).
response: Section 319 CrPC empowers the court to summon and proceed against any person not named as an accused in the charge-sheet, if it appears from the evidence adduced during trial that such person has committed an offence for which they could be tried together with the accused. In Hardeep Singh (2014), the Constitution Bench held that the test is more than a prima facie case, but less than proof beyond doubt.

instruction: Explain the legal provision, essential ingredients, and court principles regarding Section 306 CrPC (Tender of pardon to accomplice (approver)).
response: Section 306 CrPC enables the Chief Judicial Magistrate or a Metropolitan Magistrate to tender a pardon to an accomplice in offences triable exclusively by Sessions Court or punishable with imprisonment of 7 years or more, on condition of their making a full and true disclosure of the whole circumstances within their knowledge relative to the offence and all confederates.

instruction: Explain the legal provision, essential ingredients, and court principles regarding Section 389 CrPC (Suspension of sentence pending appeal and release of appellant on bail).
response: Section 389 CrPC empowers an Appellate Court to suspend the execution of the sentence or order appealed against and release the appellant on bail pending appeal, for reasons to be recorded in writing. The court balances the nature of the crime, period already undergone, and likelihood of appeal not being heard expeditiously.

instruction: Explain the legal provision, essential ingredients, and court principles regarding Section 437 CrPC (Bail in non-bailable offences by Magistrate Court).
response: Section 437 CrPC governs bail in non-bailable offences before Courts other than High Court or Sessions Court. It restricts bail if there appear reasonable grounds for believing that the accused has been guilty of an offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life, subject to exceptions for persons under 16 years of age, women, sick, or infirm persons.

instruction: Explain the legal provision, essential ingredients, and court principles regarding Order VIII Rule 1 CPC (Written Statement filing timeline).
response: Order VIII Rule 1 CPC provides that the defendant shall present a written statement of defence within thirty days from the date of service of summons. The court may extend this period for reasons recorded in writing up to ninety days. In commercial disputes governed by the Commercial Courts Act, 2015, the outer limit of 120 days is mandatory and non-extendable.

instruction: Explain the legal provision, essential ingredients, and court principles regarding Order XXXVIII Rule 5 CPC (Attachment before judgment).
response: Order XXXVIII Rule 5 CPC empowers the court to direct the defendant to furnish security or produce property, or attach property before judgment, if satisfied that the defendant, with intent to obstruct or delay execution, is about to dispose of or remove property from local court limits. It is an extraordinary power exercised with circumspection.

instruction: Explain the legal provision, essential ingredients, and court principles regarding Section 34 Arbitration Act (Setting aside of Arbitral Award).
response: Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 provides limited statutory grounds for setting aside an arbitral award, including incapacity of parties, invalid agreement, lack of proper notice, dispute outside scope of submission, arbitral composition contrary to agreement, patent illegality on the face of the award, or conflict with public policy of India.

instruction: Explain the legal provision, essential ingredients, and court principles regarding Section 37 Arbitration Act (Appeals against arbitration orders).
response: Section 37 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 provides for appeals against specified orders only: (1) refusing to refer parties to arbitration under Section 8; (2) granting or refusing interim measure under Section 9; (3) setting aside or refusing to set aside an arbitral award under Section 34. No second appeal lies from an order passed under Section 37.

instruction: Explain the legal provision, essential ingredients, and court principles regarding Section 12 Commercial Courts Act (Pre-Institution Mediation and Settlement (PIMS)).
response: Section 12A of the Commercial Courts Act, 2015 mandates that a suit which does not contemplate any urgent interim relief shall not be instituted unless the plaintiff exhausts the remedy of pre-institution mediation in accordance with the rules. In Patil Automation (2022), the Supreme Court held that Section 12A is mandatory, and suits filed without exhausting PIMS are liable to rejection under Order VII Rule 11 CPC.

instruction: Explain the legal provision, essential ingredients, and court principles regarding Section 18 Limitation Act (Effect of acknowledgment in writing of liability).
response: Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963 provides that where, before the expiration of the prescribed period of limitation for a suit or application in respect of any property or right, an acknowledgment of liability has been made in writing signed by the party against whom such property or right is claimed, a fresh period of limitation begins from the date of acknowledgment.

instruction: Explain the legal provision, essential ingredients, and court principles regarding Section 5 Limitation Act (Condonation of delay).
response: Section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1963 allows the court to admit any appeal or application (except under Order XXI CPC) after the prescribed limitation period, if the appellant or applicant satisfies the court that they had 'sufficient cause' for not preferring the appeal or application within time. The court adopts a liberal and justice-oriented approach.

instruction: Explain the legal provision, essential ingredients, and court principles regarding Section 73 Indian Contract Act (Compensation for loss or damage caused by breach of contract).
response: Section 73 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 incorporates the rule in Hadley v. Baxendale. When a contract is broken, the party suffering breach is entitled to receive compensation for any loss or damage which naturally arose in the usual course of things, or which the parties knew when they made the contract to be likely to result from the breach. Remote and indirect damages are not recoverable.

instruction: Explain the legal provision, essential ingredients, and court principles regarding Section 74 Indian Contract Act (Compensation for breach where penalty stipulated).
response: Section 74 of the Indian Contract Act provides that where a contract stipulates a sum named as liquidated damages or penalty for breach, the aggrieved party is entitled to receive reasonable compensation not exceeding the amount so named, whether or not actual damage or loss is proved to have been caused. In Kailash Nath (2015), the Supreme Court held that proof of actual loss is not dispensed with if damages can be assessed.

instruction: Explain the legal provision, essential ingredients, and court principles regarding Section 10 Specific Relief Act (Specific performance of contract mandatory post-2018).
response: Following the 2018 amendment, Section 10 of the Specific Relief Act makes specific performance of a contract mandatory rather than discretionary. The court shall enforce specific performance of a contract subject to the exceptions contained in sub-section (2) of Section 11, Section 14, and Section 16, replacing the earlier regime of damages being the primary remedy.

instruction: Explain the test for determining an 'instrumentality or agency of the State' under Article 12 of the Constitution.
response: In Ajay Hasia v. Khalid Mujib Sehravardi (1981) 1 SCC 722 and Pradeep Kumar Biswas v. Indian Institute of Chemical Biology (2002) 5 SCC 111, the Supreme Court laid down the cumulative tests to determine if a body is 'State' under Article 12: (1) Entire share capital held by the Government; (2) Deep and pervasive State control; (3) Financial assistance meeting almost entire expenditure; (4) Monopolistic status conferred or protected by the State; (5) Functions of public importance closely related to governmental functions; (6) Transfer of a government department to the corporation.

instruction: What is the scope of Article 20(3) of the Constitution regarding the right against self-incrimination?
response: Article 20(3) provides that 'no person accused of any offence shall be compelled to be a witness against himself'. Its essential ingredients are: (1) The person must be accused of an offence at the time of compulsion; (2) There must be compulsion to be a witness; (3) The compulsion must be to give evidence against himself. In Selvi v. State of Karnataka (2010) 7 SCC 263, the Supreme Court held that involuntary administration of narco-analysis, polygraph tests, or BEAP (brain mapping) violates Article 20(3) as well as the right to privacy under Article 21.

instruction: Explain the Doctrine of Eclipse under Article 13(1) of the Constitution.
response: The Doctrine of Eclipse, propounded in Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v. State of M.P. (1955), applies to pre-constitutional laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights under Article 13(1). Such laws do not become void ab initio or completely dead; rather, they remain dormant and overshadowed ('eclipsed') by the fundamental right to the extent of inconsistency. If a subsequent constitutional amendment removes the inconsistency, the shadow is lifted and the law becomes operative again without fresh enactment.

instruction: What is the plenary scope of Article 142 of the Constitution of India?
response: Article 142(1) empowers the Supreme Court to pass such decree or order as is necessary for doing 'complete justice' in any cause or matter pending before it. It is an inherent, extraordinary equitable power that is not fettered by ordinary statutory provisions, provided it does not contravene express constitutional prohibitions or fundamental principles of justice (as affirmed in Union Carbide Corp. v. Union of India and Supreme Court Bar Association v. Union of India).

instruction: What are the essential ingredients of medical negligence under Section 304A IPC as laid down in Jacob Mathew v. State of Punjab (2005)?
response: In Jacob Mathew v. State of Punjab (2005) 6 SCC 1, the Supreme Court held that to prosecute a medical professional under Section 304A IPC for causing death by negligence: (1) The negligence must be 'gross' (culpable rashness or gross negligence), not merely an error of judgment; (2) The standard is that of an ordinary competent doctor exercising reasonable skill; (3) A criminal complaint should not be entertained without an independent medical opinion from a competent government doctor affirming gross negligence.

instruction: Explain the ingredients of Abetment of Suicide under Section 306 IPC.
response: Under Section 306 IPC, whoever abets the commission of suicide is punishable with imprisonment up to ten years and fine. Abetment requires the ingredients of Section 107 IPC: instigation, conspiracy, or intentional aiding. In Sanju v. State of M.P. (2002) and Geo Varghese v. State of Rajasthan (2021), the Supreme Court reiterated that there must be an active, proximate act or direct instigation by the accused with mens rea (guilty intention) leaving the deceased with no option but to commit suicide.

instruction: What are the statutory exceptions to Defamation under Section 499 of the Indian Penal Code?
response: Section 499 IPC contains ten statutory exceptions where imputations do not amount to criminal defamation: (1) Imputation of truth made for public good; (2) Public conduct of public servants; (3) Conduct of any person touching any public question; (4) Publication of substantially true reports of court proceedings; (5) Merits of case decided in court or conduct of witnesses; (6) Merits of public performance; (7) Censure passed in good faith by person having lawful authority; (8) Accusation preferred in good faith to authorized person; (9) Imputation made in good faith for protection of interests; (10) Caution intended for good of person or public.

instruction: Distinguish between Hurt (Section 319 IPC) and Grievous Hurt (Section 320 IPC).
response: Hurt (Section 319 IPC) involves causing bodily pain, disease, or infirmity to any person. Grievous Hurt (Section 320 IPC) is a designated aggravated form encompassing eight specific statutory categories: (1) Emasculation; (2) Permanent privation of sight of either eye; (3) Permanent privation of hearing of either ear; (4) Privation of any member or joint; (5) Destruction or permanent impairing of powers of any member or joint; (6) Permanent disfiguration of head or face; (7) Fracture or dislocation of a bone or tooth; (8) Any hurt which endangers life or causes severe bodily pain or inability to follow ordinary pursuits for 20 days.

instruction: Explain the Doctrine of Res Gestae under Section 6 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872.
response: Section 6 of the Indian Evidence Act (and Section 4 of BSA) incorporates the Doctrine of Res Gestae ('things done'). It provides that facts which, though not in issue, are so connected with a fact in issue as to form part of the same transaction, are relevant, whether they occurred at the same time and place or at different times and places. The statements or acts must be spontaneous and contemporaneous with the event, ruling out fabrication or concoction.

instruction: What is the evidentiary value of a Hostile Witness under Section 154 of the Indian Evidence Act?
response: In Sat Paul v. Delhi Administration (1976) and Neeraj Dutta v. State (Govt. of NCT of Delhi) (2023), the Supreme Court held that the testimony of a hostile witness (a witness declared hostile under Section 154) is not completely effaced or discarded from the record. The court can accept that portion of the evidence of a hostile witness which is found to be trustworthy and corroborated by other independent evidence, and can rely upon it for conviction as well as acquittal.

instruction: What are the rules regarding the Plea of Alibi under Section 11 of the Indian Evidence Act?
response: The Plea of Alibi ('elsewhere') under Section 11 IEA is an assertion by the accused that they were physically present at a place so far removed from the crime scene that their participation in the crime was physically impossible. The burden of proving an alibi rests strictly upon the accused under Section 103 of the Evidence Act. In Binay Kumar Singh (1997), the Supreme Court held that the alibi must be established with absolute certainty showing physical impossibility of presence.

instruction: Explain the Best Evidence Rule under Section 91 of the Indian Evidence Act.
response: Section 91 of the Indian Evidence Act embodies the Best Evidence Rule: when the terms of a contract, grant, or other disposition of property have been reduced to the form of a document, no evidence shall be given in proof of the terms of such contract or grant except the document itself, or secondary evidence where admissible under Section 65. Oral evidence is completely excluded to prove the contents of such written documents.

instruction: What is the difference between a Decree and an Order under Section 2(2) and Section 2(14) of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908?
response: Under Section 2(2) CPC, a 'decree' is the formal expression of an adjudication which conclusively determines the rights of the parties with regard to all or any of the matters in controversy in the suit; it may be preliminary or final, and an appeal lies against every decree as of right under Section 96. Under Section 2(14) CPC, an 'order' is the formal expression of any decision of a Civil Court which is not a decree; an order is appealable only if specifically provided under Section 104 and Order XLIII CPC.

instruction: What are the prerequisites for Amendment of Pleadings under Order VI Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908?
response: Under Order VI Rule 17 CPC, the court may at any stage allow either party to alter or amend their pleadings in such manner as may be necessary for determining the real question in controversy between the parties. However, the proviso inserted by the 2002 Amendment mandates that no application for amendment shall be allowed after the trial has commenced, unless the court concludes that in spite of due diligence, the party could not have raised the matter before commencement of trial.

instruction: Explain Section 80 CPC regarding notice to the Government prior to instituting a civil suit.
response: Section 80(1) CPC mandates that no suit shall be instituted against the Government or against a public officer in respect of any act purporting to be done in their official capacity, until the expiration of two months next after a written notice has been delivered or left at their office. Section 80(2) provides an exception: a suit to obtain urgent and immediate relief may be instituted with the leave of the court without serving two months notice, but no ex-parte interim relief can be granted without giving reasonable opportunity to show cause.

instruction: What are the three tiers of consumer dispute redressal commissions under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019?
response: Under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (as modified by 2021 Rules), the pecuniary jurisdictions are: (1) District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission: entertains complaints where the value of goods or services paid as consideration does not exceed Rs. 50 Lakhs; (2) State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission: entertains complaints where consideration exceeds Rs. 50 Lakhs but does not exceed Rs. 2 Crores, as well as appeals against District Commission orders; (3) National Commission (NCDRC): entertains complaints exceeding Rs. 2 Crores and appellate/revisional jurisdiction.

instruction: What are the remedies available to an allottee under Section 18 of the Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act (RERA), 2016 for delay in possession?
response: Under Section 18 of RERA, 2016, if a promoter fails to complete or give possession of an apartment, plot, or building in accordance with the terms of the agreement for sale by the specified date: (1) The allottee wishing to withdraw from the project is entitled to a full refund of the amount paid along with interest at the prescribed rate and compensation; (2) If the allottee does not withdraw, the promoter must pay monthly interest for every month of delay till possession is handed over.

instruction: What is the effect of Moratorium under Section 14 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (IBC)?
response: Upon admission of a Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) application under Section 7, 9, or 10, the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT) declares a moratorium under Section 14 IBC prohibiting: (a) the institution of suits or continuation of pending proceedings against the corporate debtor; (b) transferring, encumbering, or alienating any assets; (c) any action to foreclose, recover, or enforce security interest; (d) recovery of any property by an owner or lessor where occupied by the corporate debtor.

1. That the allegations made in the notice under reply are entirely false, frivolous, baseless, and vehemently denied.
2. That my client never borrowed any loan amount of Rs. [AMOUNT]/- from your client nor was any legally enforceable debt or liability due.
3. That the cheque in question was handed over strictly as a blank security cheque in connection with an incomplete business transaction, which your client dishonestly retained and unauthorizedly filled up.
4. That no offence under Section 138 NI Act or Section 420 IPC has been committed. Your client is advised to refrain from initiating malicious prosecution, failing which my client shall prosecute your client for perjury, malicious proceedings, and damages.

instruction: What are the twin conditions for bail under Section 45 of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 (PMLA)?
response: Under Section 45(1) of the PMLA, 2002, bail cannot be granted for an offence under the Act unless: (1) The Public Prosecutor has been given an opportunity to oppose the bail application; and (2) Where the Public Prosecutor opposes, the Court is satisfied that there are reasonable grounds for believing that the accused is 'not guilty of such offence' and that they are 'not likely to commit any offence while on bail'. In Vijay Madanlal Choudhary v. Union of India (2022), the Supreme Court upheld the constitutionality of these twin conditions.

instruction: What is the mandatory procedure for personal search under Section 50 of the NDPS Act, 1985?
response: Section 50 of the NDPS Act mandates that before searching a person suspected of possessing contraband, the authorized officer must inform the person of their statutory right to be searched in the presence of a Gazetted Officer or a Magistrate. In Vijaysinh Chandubha Jadeja v. State of Gujarat (2011 5-judge bench), the Supreme Court held that strict compliance with Section 50 is mandatory; failure to apprise the suspect of this right vitiates the search and recovery, rendering the prosecution fatal.

instruction: Explain corporate criminal liability under Section 141 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881.
response: Section 141 NI Act provides for vicarious criminal liability of company officials when a cheque bounced is issued by a company. For a Director or official to be held liable: (1) The company must be arrayed as a prime accused (Aneeta Hada v. Godfather Travels, 2012); (2) Specific averments must be made in the complaint demonstrating that at the time the offence was committed, the person was 'in charge of, and responsible to the company for the conduct of the business of the company' (SMS Pharmaceuticals, 2005). Independent or non-executive directors are not automatically vicariously liable.

instruction: What is the mandatory presumption under Section 29 of the POCSO Act, 2012?
response: Section 29 of the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, 2012 creates a statutory reverse burden of proof. Where a person is prosecuted for committing or abetting an offence under Sections 3, 5, 7, or 9, the Special Court 'shall presume' that the accused has committed or abetted the offence, once foundational facts demonstrating physical involvement with the child are prima facie established by the prosecution. The accused can rebut this presumption on a preponderance of probabilities.

instruction: Explain the Doctrine of Lis Pendens under Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882.
response: Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act codifies the maxim 'pendente lite nihil innovetur' (during litigation, nothing new should be introduced). It provides that during the pendency in any competent court of any suit or proceeding which is not collusive and in which any right to immovable property is directly and specifically in question, the property cannot be transferred or otherwise dealt with by any party to the suit so as to affect the rights of any other party thereto under any decree or order which may be made therein, except with the authority of the court.

instruction: What are the essentials of the Doctrine of Part Performance under Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882?
response: Section 53A TPA provides an equitable shield of defence to a transferee. Essentials are: (1) A written contract to transfer immovable property signed by the transferor; (2) The terms can be ascertained with reasonable certainty; (3) The transferee has taken possession of the property in part performance of the contract, or being already in possession continues in possession and has done some act in furtherance; (4) The transferee has performed or is willing to perform their part of the contract. Following the 2001 amendment, the contract must be registered to claim protection under Section 53A.

instruction: What are the rights of a Hindu daughter as a Coparcener under Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act post-2005 as settled in Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma (2020)?
response: In Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma (2020) 9 SCC 1, a 3-judge bench of the Supreme Court held that under amended Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, a daughter becomes a coparcener by birth in her own right in the same manner as a son. The Court held that this right is conferred retroactively by birth; hence, it is not necessary that the father coparcener was alive on 9th September 2005 when the Amendment Act came into force. Dispositions and alienations concluded prior to 20th December 2004 remain unaffected.

instruction: What are the requirements for valid execution and attestation of an unprivileged Will under Section 63 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925?
response: Under Section 63 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925: (1) The testator must sign or affix their mark to the Will, or have it signed by another person in their presence and direction; (2) The signature or mark must appear intended to give effect to the writing as a Will; (3) The Will must be attested by two or more witnesses, each of whom must have seen the testator sign or received a personal acknowledgment of signature; (4) Each witness must sign the Will in the presence of the testator (though witnesses need not sign simultaneously).

instruction: What is the distinction between Liquidated Damages and Penalty under Section 74 of the Indian Contract Act?
response: Under English law, liquidated damages (pre-estimate of loss) are enforceable, while penalties (in terrorem sums) are void. Under Indian law (Section 74 Contract Act), this distinction is abolished: the court will award only 'reasonable compensation' not exceeding the named amount, irrespective of whether the stipulated sum is termed liquidated damages or a penalty. In Fateh Chand v. Balkishan Dass (1964) and ONGC v. Saw Pipes (2003), the Supreme Court affirmed that the named sum represents the maximum ceiling.

instruction: What is the limitation period for filing a suit for Specific Performance of an agreement to sell under Article 54 of the Limitation Act, 1963?
response: Under Article 54 of the Schedule to the Limitation Act, 1963, the limitation period for a suit for specific performance is 3 (three) years. Time begins to run from: (1) The date fixed for the performance of the contract; or (2) If no date is fixed, when the plaintiff has notice that performance is refused by the defendant.

instruction: Explain the Kompetenz-Kompetenz principle under Section 16 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996.
response: Section 16 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act codifies the internationally recognized doctrine of 'Kompetenz-Kompetenz'. It empowers the Arbitral Tribunal to rule on its own jurisdiction, including ruling on any objections with respect to the existence or validity of the arbitration agreement. An arbitration clause which forms part of a contract shall be treated as an agreement independent of the other terms of the contract, and a decision by the tribunal that the contract is null and void shall not entail ipso jure the invalidity of the arbitration clause.

instruction: What is the statutory time limit for completing arbitral proceedings under Section 29A of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996?
response: Section 29A mandates that the arbitral award in matters other than international commercial arbitration must be made within twelve (12) months from the date of completion of pleadings under Section 23(4). The parties may by mutual consent extend this period for a further term not exceeding six (6) months. If the award is not made within the period or extended period, the mandate of the arbitrator terminates, unless extended by the Court on an application made by either party for sufficient cause.

Summarize the landmark bail categories laid down in Satender Kumar Antil v. CBI (2022).
response: In Satender Kumar Antil v. CBI (2022) 10 SCC 51, the Supreme Court categorized criminal offences into four distinct brackets to regulate bail and prevent unnecessary arrests: Category A: Offences punishable up to 7 years (ordinary arrest not required; follow Section 41/41A CrPC; on summons appearance, bail to be decided without remand); Category B: Offences punishable with death, life imprisonment, or exceeding 7 years (bail on merits); Category C: Special Acts with statutory negative bail covenants such as NDPS (S. 37), PMLA (S. 45), UAPA (S. 43D(5)); Category D: Economic offences not covered by Special Acts (gravity of economic loss assessed with individual merits).

instruction: What are the uniform maintenance guidelines established in Rajnesh v. Neha (2020)?
response: In Rajnesh v. Neha (2020) 13 SCC 732, the Supreme Court formulated comprehensive guidelines to overcome overlapping maintenance claims across Section 125 CrPC, PWDVA, and Hindu Marriage Act: (1) Mandatory filing of an Affidavit of Assets and Liabilities by both spouses; (2) Maintenance must be awarded from the date of filing the application; (3) Overlapping maintenance orders in different proceedings must be adjusted and set off against each other; (4) Enforcement of maintenance orders can be executed as a money decree under CPC or Section 421/125(3) CrPC including civil detention.

instruction: Summarize the 5-judge Constitution Bench ruling in High Court Bar Association, Allahabad v. State of U.P. (2024) regarding stay orders.
response: In High Court Bar Association, Allahabad v. State of U.P. (2024), a 5-judge Constitution Bench expressly overruled the 2018 ruling in Asian Resurfacing. The Court held that interim stay orders granted by High Courts in civil and criminal proceedings do not automatically expire or vacate after six months without judicial determination. Constitutional courts cannot set automatic vacation deadlines under Article 142 as it infringes upon judicial discretion and causes prejudice to bona fide litigants.
