instruction: Explain the essential conditions for grant of Anticipatory Bail under Section 438 CrPC as settled in Gurbaksh Singh Sibbia v. State of Punjab (1980).
response: In Gurbaksh Singh Sibbia v. State of Punjab (1980) 2 SCC 565 (affirmed by Constitution Bench in Sushila Aggarwal v. State (NCT of Delhi), 2020), the Supreme Court laid down foundational principles for Section 438 CrPC: (1) Anticipatory bail cannot be circumscribed by rigid fetters not found in the statute; (2) The applicant must demonstrate a reasonable belief and apprehension of arrest on accusations of having committed a non-bailable offence, not mere vague fear; (3) Anticipatory bail should not ordinarily be limited to a fixed time period and may continue till the conclusion of trial; (4) The court balances personal liberty under Article 21 with legitimate investigative interests.

instruction: What is the scope of Section 300 CrPC and Article 20(2) regarding Double Jeopardy (Autrefois Acquit and Autrefois Convict)?
response: Article 20(2) provides that no person shall be prosecuted and punished for the same offence more than once. Section 300 CrPC is wider in scope: A person who has once been tried by a court of competent jurisdiction for an offence and convicted or acquitted of such offence shall, while such conviction or acquittal remains in force, not be liable to be tried again for the same offence, nor on the same facts for any other offence for which a different charge might have been made under Section 221(1) CrPC. Autrefois convict bars second prosecution after conviction; autrefois acquit bars second prosecution after acquittal.

instruction: Explain the concept of 'Per Incuriam' and 'Sub Silentio' in Indian Judicial Precedents.
response: 'Per incuriam' ('through lack of care') refers to a judicial decision rendered in ignorance or forgetfulness of a binding statutory provision or a binding precedent of a superior court. A decision per incuriam does not carry precedential authority and is not binding on subsequent benches. 'Sub silentio' occurs where a particular point of law involved in the decision is not perceived or addressed by the court and passes without argument or express judicial determination; such unargued assumptions do not establish binding ratio decidendi.

instruction: What is the procedure for Trial of Warrant Cases by Magistrates instituted on a police report under Sections 238 to 243 CrPC?
response: The procedure comprises: (1) Compliance with Section 207 (supply of documents, S. 238); (2) Discharge of accused under Section 239 if allegations are groundless; (3) Framing of formal charge under Section 240 if ground exists for presuming accused committed the offence; (4) Plea of accused (S. 241); (5) Evidence for prosecution under Section 242 (examination of witnesses); (6) Cross-examination of prosecution witnesses; (7) Examination of accused under Section 313; (8) Defence evidence under Section 243; (9) Arguments and judgment of acquittal or conviction under Section 248.

instruction: What are the rules regarding Inherent Powers of the Court under Section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908?
response: Section 151 CPC provides that nothing in the Code shall be deemed to limit or otherwise affect the inherent power of the Court to make such orders as may be necessary for the ends of justice or to prevent abuse of the process of the Court. In Manohar Lal Chopra v. Rai Raja Seth Hiralal (1962), the Supreme Court clarified: (1) Inherent powers are not substantive powers conferring jurisdiction where none exists; (2) They cannot be exercised in conflict with or to override express statutory provisions; (3) They are invoked to meet unforeseen contingencies and advance substantial justice.

instruction: Explain the requirements of Notice under Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882.
response: Section 106 TPA regulates termination of month-to-month leases: (1) In absence of contract or local law, a lease of immovable property for agricultural or manufacturing purposes is deemed to be year-to-year terminable by six months notice; (2) Leases for any other purpose are deemed month-to-month terminable by fifteen days notice; (3) Notice must be in writing, signed by the lessor or authorized agent, and delivered either personally or by registered post; (4) Post-2002 amendment, the notice period begins from the date of receipt of notice.

instruction: What is the doctrine of Adverse Possession under Articles 64 and 65 of the Limitation Act, 1963?
response: Under Article 65 of the Limitation Act, the limitation period for recovering possession of immovable property based on title is 12 years from the date the possession of the defendant becomes adverse to the plaintiff. Adverse possession requires 'nec vi, nec clam, nec precario' (possession must be open, notorious, continuous, and hostile to the true owner). In Ravinder Kaur Grewal v. Manjit Kaur (2019 3-judge bench), the Supreme Court held that adverse possession can be used not only as a shield by a defendant but also as a sword by a plaintiff to protect possession or declare title.

instruction: What is the procedure for Grant of Succession Certificate under Section 372 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925?
response: A Succession Certificate under Part X of the Indian Succession Act is issued by the District Court or Civil Judge for the realization of debts and securities of a deceased person. The petition must set out the time of death, family pedigree, ordinary residence of deceased, absence of any Will, and specific schedule of debts/securities. Citation is published in newspapers inviting objections. The court conducts a summary inquiry into prima facie entitlement. The certificate holder is legally empowered to receive interest, dividends, and negotiate the securities.

instruction: What is the scope of Section 340 CrPC for prosecution of offences against public justice (perjury)?
response: Section 340 CrPC outlines the procedure for prosecuting offences enumerated in Section 195(1)(b) CrPC, including perjury (S. 193 IPC) and fabricating false evidence (S. 192 IPC) committed in or in relation to a proceeding in any court. The court conducts a preliminary inquiry and must record a finding that it is 'expedient in the interests of justice' to prosecute the offender. In Iqbal Singh Marwah v. Meenakshi Marwah (2005 5-judge bench), the Supreme Court held that Section 195(1)(b)(ii) applies only when the forgery was committed after the document was produced in court, and not when forged prior to filing.

instruction: Explain the concept of 'Custody Death' and inquiry under Section 176(1A) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.
response: Section 176(1A) CrPC was inserted in 2005 to mandate that in any case where any person dies, disappears, or where rape is alleged to have been committed on any woman while in the custody of the police or in any other custody authorized by court, a mandatory judicial inquiry shall be held by the Judicial Magistrate or Metropolitan Magistrate, in addition to the ordinary police investigation. The Magistrate records statements and directs post-mortem examination within 24 hours of death.

instruction: What are the rules governing Confessions under Section 24, 25, and 26 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872?
response: Under IEA: Section 24 renders irrelevant any confession made by an accused person if caused by any inducement, threat, or promise proceeding from a person in authority. Section 25 creates an absolute statutory prohibition: no confession made to a police officer shall be proved as against a person accused of any offence. Section 26 mandates that no confession made by any person while in police custody shall be proved, unless made in the immediate presence of a Magistrate.

instruction: What is the purpose of Section 482 CrPC and its non-applicability to interlocutory orders?
response: Section 482 CrPC preserves the High Court's inherent power to prevent abuse of the process of any court and to secure the ends of justice. It is an extraordinary power used sparingly with circumspection. It cannot be exercised to bypass express statutory bars, such as Section 397(2) CrPC which bars revision against interlocutory orders, unless the order is completely without jurisdiction or causes exceptional miscarriage of justice.

instruction: What is the distinction between Section 138 of the NI Act and Section 420 IPC?
response: Section 138 NI Act is a regulatory offence where mens rea is not an essential ingredient; dishonour of cheque due to insufficient funds after statutory notice constitutes the offence. Section 420 IPC (Cheating) requires fraudulent or dishonest intention from the very inception of the transaction. A mere dishonour of a cheque does not attract Section 420 IPC unless the complainant proves that the accused had no intention to honour the commitment when the cheque was issued.

instruction: What is a 'Zero FIR' and how does it function in Indian criminal procedure?
response: A Zero FIR is an FIR that can be registered by any police station, irrespective of territorial jurisdiction, upon receiving information about a cognizable offence. It is assigned the number '0' (zero) and entered into the register. The police station conducts initial urgent investigation (such as medical examination or crime scene preservation) and immediately transfers the case diary and FIR to the jurisdictional police station for regular investigation under Section 170 CrPC (now codified under Section 173 BNSS).

instruction: What is the difference between Order VII Rule 10 and Order VII Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908?
response: Order VII Rule 10 CPC provides for 'Return of Plaint' when the court lacks territorial or pecuniary jurisdiction; the plaint is returned with an endorsement of presentation and return dates to be presented before the proper court. Order VII Rule 11 CPC provides for 'Rejection of Plaint' on statutory grounds such as failure to disclose a cause of action, undervaluation, or legal bar; rejection operates as a deemed decree under Section 2(2) and is appealable.

instruction: What are the rules for filing a Review Application under Order XLVII Rule 1 CPC?
response: Under Order XLVII Rule 1 CPC, a party aggrieved by a decree or order from which an appeal is allowed but no appeal has been preferred, or from which no appeal is allowed, may apply for review on three strict grounds: (1) Discovery of new and important matter or evidence which after exercise of due diligence was not within their knowledge; (2) Some mistake or error apparent on the face of the record; (3) Any other sufficient reason (ejusdem generis with the first two). A review cannot be an appeal in disguise.

instruction: Explain the concept of 'Lis Mota' in the Law of Evidence.
response: 'Lis Mota' ('dispute arisen') is a Latin doctrine in the law of evidence providing that statements of deceased persons or public records regarding family pedigree, public rights, or customs are admissible under Section 32(5) and (6) of the Evidence Act only if they were made 'ante litem motam'—that is, before the controversy or dispute in question arose. Statements made post litem motam are excluded because of the risk of bias and interest.

instruction: What is the effect of Section 144 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 regarding Restitution?
response: Section 144 CPC codifies the doctrine of Restitution based on the maxim 'actus curiae neminem gravabit' (the act of the court shall prejudice no one). Where a decree or order is varied or reversed in appeal, revision, or review, the court of first instance shall, on application, cause restitution to be made to the party entitled, placing them in the same position they would have occupied but for such decree or order, including ordering mesne profits and interest.

instruction: What is a 'Speaking Order' in Administrative Law?
response: A 'Speaking Order' (reasoned order) is an order that contains the reasons and grounds upon which the administrative or quasi-judicial decision is founded. The recording of reasons is a fundamental facet of natural justice (third pillar alongside audi alteram partem and nemo judex in causa sua). A reasoned order assures the litigant that their case was considered, acts as a check against arbitrariness, and enables the appellate/writ court to exercise effective judicial review.

instruction: What are the essentials of Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 regarding Second Appeals?
response: Under Section 100 CPC, a Second Appeal lies to the High Court from an appellate decree passed by a subordinate court strictly on a 'substantial question of law' formulated by the High Court. A second appeal does not lie on mere questions of fact or concurrent findings of fact unless the finding is perverse, based on no evidence, or arrived at by ignoring material evidence on record.

instruction: Explain the concept of 'Waiver' versus 'Estoppel' in Indian Law.
response: Waiver is the intentional and voluntary relinquishment or abandonment of a known existing legal right or advantage; it arises from the conscious choice of the party entitled to the right. Estoppel is an equitable rule of evidence (Section 115 IEA) which prevents a party from asserting something contrary to what is implied by their previous action, representation, or statement, because another party has altered their position relying on that representation.

instruction: What is the procedure for Examination of Witnesses under Sections 137 and 138 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872?
response: Section 137 IEA defines three stages of examination: (1) Examination-in-chief (by the party who calls the witness); (2) Cross-examination (by the adverse party); (3) Re-examination (by the calling party to explain matters referred to in cross-examination). Section 138 prescribes the mandatory order: witness must first be examined-in-chief, then cross-examined, and then re-examined. Cross-examination need not be confined to facts testified to in chief, provided they are relevant.

instruction: What constitutes 'Unlawful Assembly' under Section 141 of the Indian Penal Code?
response: An assembly of five or more persons is an 'unlawful assembly' under Section 141 IPC if their common object is: (1) To overawe by criminal force the Central or State Government or Parliament or public servant; (2) To resist the execution of any law or legal process; (3) To commit any mischief, criminal trespass, or other offence; (4) By means of criminal force to take or obtain possession of property or enforce any right; (5) To compel any person to do what they are not legally bound to do.

instruction: What is the scope of Section 12 of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971?
response: Section 12 of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 prescribes the punishment for civil or criminal contempt with simple imprisonment up to six months or fine up to two thousand rupees or both. The proviso provides that the accused may be discharged or punishment remitted upon apology being made to the satisfaction of the court, provided the apology is bona fide and not a mere defensive stratagem.

instruction: What are the rules regarding Injunction against encashment of Bank Guarantees in Indian Law?
response: As settled in U.P. State Sugar Corp. v. Sumac International Ltd. (1997) and Svenska Handelsbanken, courts will not grant an injunction restraining encashment of an unconditional bank guarantee unless: (1) There is established egregious fraud of a serious nature of which the bank has notice; or (2) Special equities exist where irretrievable injustice or harm would be caused to the parties. A dispute under the underlying commercial contract is not a ground for restraining encashment.

instruction: What is the doctrine of 'Separation of Powers' in the Constitution of India as settled in Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975)?
response: In Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975) Supp SCC 1, the Supreme Court held that the Indian Constitution does not recognise a rigid doctrine of separation of powers as in the US Constitution, but embodies a broad functional division of powers between the Legislature, Executive, and Judiciary with checks and balances. The amending power under Article 368 cannot be used by the Legislature to exercise judicial power or validate an election by declaration, as judicial adjudication of disputes is part of the basic structure.
